title: Human verification gates in the sprint lifecycle state machine

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL PASS â€” QA1 audit round 1, Sprint 12, commit 26bb3fa (HEAD), clean
tree for every audited path (the only dirty file is sprint-7's definition,
unrelated). Sprint file read fresh and in full, including the Q1â€“Q5 design and
Dev Notes, before this verdict. CLAUDE.md re-read at this commit, since this
diff amends it.

One required fix. It is a documentation fix inside requirement 1's own
deliverable, not a code change, and everything else in this sprint passed â€”
much of it verified by running the thing rather than reading it.

METHOD, STATED UP FRONT BECAUSE IT IS UNUSUAL FOR ME
This sprint changes the mechanism my own verdicts are recorded through, so
reading the diff was not sufficient. I exercised the new behaviour in two
throwaway sandboxes under the session scratchpad â€” a copy of the script with
its own `docs/sprints/` tree, exactly the discipline `smoke_test.sh` uses â€”
and confirmed each claim against the resulting state JSON rather than against
the script's own success messages. This is still static review: it is a
script's behaviour, read by running it, with no deployed product anywhere
near it. This repository's `docs/sprints/` was never written to; I hashed it
before and after every run that could plausibly have touched it and it is
byte-identical.

===================================================================
THE FOUR THINGS I WAS ASKED TO CHECK CLOSELY
===================================================================

**1. `cmd_complete`'s missing-gate checks â€” BOTH BRANCHES CONFIRMED, BY NAME.**

Declared gate, no result recorded:
  ERROR: Sprint is not ready to close:
    - Gate 3 (human AT pass, e.g. NVDA) is declared but has no recorded result

Declared gate whose last result was CONDITIONAL:
  ERROR: Sprint is not ready to close:
    - Gate 3 (human AT pass, e.g. NVDA) last recorded CONDITIONAL, needs a
      fresh PASS

Both refuse, both name the gate, and the two cases are distinguishable in the
message exactly as Q4's design says. An undeclared gate contributes nothing to
`missing` â€” verified on a sprint that declared neither, which closed with the
pre-Sprint-12 message unchanged. A sprint declaring both gates closes with
both named in the confirmation line, which is a real improvement: the close
record now says what was actually confirmed.

**2. The reopen edge â€” VERIFIED AGAINST THE STATE JSON, NOT THE MESSAGES.**

Recorded CONDITIONAL on a declared gate3 while the sandbox sprint sat at
`complete_ready`. Read back from `sprint-1.json` directly:

  phase                 : dev_build          <- not groundtruth_live
  qa1_audit_file_hash   : None               <- cleared
  qa1_audited_tree_hash : None               <- cleared
  qa1_audit_result      : PASS               <- deliberately kept, per Q3
  groundtruth_result    : PASS               <- untouched
  live_test_rounds      : 1                  <- not incremented
  last_shipped_commit   : 4ee58cb45886       <- preserved, per Q3

History, in full, after the reopen:

  system       sprint_started
  dev-team     human_gate_declared    'Gate 3 (human AT pass, e.g. NVDA)'
  qa1          audit                  'PASS: ok'
  dev-team     dev_agreed_done
  pipeman      shipped                'commit=4ee58cb4â€¦'
  groundtruth  live_test              'PASS: ok'
  dev-team     human_gate_recorded    'gate3_nvda: CONDITIONAL: â€¦'
  dev-team     human_gate_reopened    'Gate 3 â€¦ recorded CONDITIONAL, reâ€¦'

GroundTruth's evidence is intact on every axis I could think to check:
exactly **one** `live_test` event, its verdict still `PASS`, zero `live_test`
entries carrying FAIL or CONDITIONAL, `groundtruth_result` and
`live_test_rounds` unchanged, and the reopen recorded as its own distinct
event naming the gate and the reason. Nothing was relabeled, duplicated, or
fabricated. This is the specific misrepresentation Q1's constraint was written
to prevent â€” a sprint recorded as having failed a live test it did not fail â€”
and the implementation avoids it by construction rather than by convention.

**3. `override --gate gate3|gate4` â€” GUARDS ENFORCED, NO SILENT NO-OP.**

  wrong --confirm value ...... refused ("must be exactly the literal word
                               OVERRIDE, typed deliberately")
  --confirm omitted .......... argparse refuses (required)
  --reason "" ................ refused
  --reason "   " ............. refused (whitespace-only is not non-empty)
  --gate gate5 ............... argparse refuses, choices listed
  undeclare a never-declared
    gate ..................... refused: "Gate 4 (legal-content review) is not
                               declared for sprint 1. Nothing to undeclare."

That last one is the specific thing asked about and it is a genuine refusal,
not a no-op that prints success. The guards are the *same* ones the hash
overrides use â€” the reason/confirm validation sits above the branch, so
gate3/gate4 inherit it rather than re-implementing it, which is why they
cannot drift apart later.

A successful undeclare preserves the history, as Q2 requires:
  human_gates.gate3_nvda: {"declared": false, "result": "CONDITIONAL",
                           "rounds": 1}
  history: actor=human-override, event=human_gate_undeclared,
           detail='reason=â€¦ | gate=â€¦ | prior_result=CONDITIONAL |
                   prior_rounds=1'
The requirement stops applying; the record of what the gate found does not
disappear. After undeclaring, `complete` no longer lists that gate and the
close confirmation correctly omits it.

**4. Backward compatibility â€” VERIFIED ON THE REAL STATE FILES.**

Copied all ten real state files (sprints 1â€“5, 8â€“12) into a second sandbox and
ran every command against them. **None of them has a `human_gates` key** â€”
which also confirms requirement 9: nothing was backfilled into a closed
sprint's state.

  status on 1,2,3,4,5,8,9,10,11,12 ....... all rc=0
  status --verbose ....................... rc=0
  list ................................... rc=0
  gates .................................. rc=0
  complete on a legacy sprint ............ refuses on phase, gate checks
                                           contribute nothing â€” behaviour
                                           identical to before this sprint
  declare-gate on a complete sprint ...... clean refusal, not a KeyError
  record-gate on a complete sprint ....... clean refusal
  declare-gate on an aborted sprint ...... clean refusal
  override --gate gate3 on a legacy file . clean refusal
  declare-gate on a live legacy sprint ... backfills correctly:
    {"gate3_nvda": {"declared": true, "result": null, "rounds": 0},
     "gate4_legal": {"declared": false, "result": null, "rounds": 0}}
  record-gate on that same file .......... works

Worth noting as the neatest test case available: **sprint-12's own state file
has no `human_gates` key**, because `start` ran before this code existed. The
sprint that introduces the field is itself a legacy file for its own commands,
and it handles it. That is a better backward-compatibility test than anything
that could have been contrived.

===================================================================
THE REST OF GATE 1
===================================================================

**Requirement 1 â€” the design, and whether the code does what it says.** The
design answers all five questions with rationale, including the two questions
answered "no new mechanism" (Q5, and Q3's decision *not* to reset
`last_shipped_commit` or `groundtruth_result`), which is what the requirement
asks for. Every behavioural claim I tested matched: the dev_build target and
not groundtruth_live, hash nulling, GroundTruth preservation, idempotent
declare, the absence of an undeclare subcommand, the closed two-entry
`GATE_KEYS`, and the mid-build FAIL that blocks completion without reopening
anything (`reopen events: 0`, phase still `dev_build`). Q1's rejected
alternative is argued rather than asserted, and the claim that no new phase
string was introduced is true â€” I checked; the seven pre-existing phase
literals are untouched.

**Requirement 2 â€” covered above.** `get_gate()` is the single defensive
accessor and both new commands `setdefault` before touching a gate.

**Requirement 3 â€” smoke_test.sh, RUN IN FULL, PASSING.**
  ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED â€” exit 0, 48 checks, 0 failures.
The pre-Sprint-12 suite, run as a control in the same environment: exit 0,
32 checks, 0 failures. Diffing the check names between the two runs:
**no pre-existing check was dropped or renamed; 16 new checks were added.**
The required cases are all present and are real assertions rather than
substring checks on success messages â€” the reopen test reads the state file
directly for the nulled hashes and counts `live_test` FAIL entries in history,
which is exactly the right way to test that property and is the same thing I
did independently.

**Requirement 4 â€” sandbox discipline preserved, verified empirically.** Every
new test runs after the existing `cd "$SANDBOX"`; all `docs/sprints` paths in
the new block are relative and therefore inside the sandbox; `REPO_ROOT` is
still used only to copy the script and template out. I hashed this repo's
`docs/sprints/` before and after a full run: identical. The header's warning
about the two historical destructions is intact.

**Requirements 5 and 6 â€” CLAUDE.md.** The lifecycle diagram now carries
`/sprint-declare-gate` and `/sprint-record-gate` and a "PASS on every declared
gate" edge. The `Open proposal` section is updated honestly â€” it says which
half Sprint 12 retires (the "needs a real design" objection, now with a
worked, tested precedent) and which half stays open (the ARIA-specific
`groundtruth_live -> qa1_audit` transition, explicitly out of scope). It does
not overclaim. The tooling-sprint guidance is corrected, and the correction is
right on the facts: `cmd_complete` does require `groundtruth_result == "PASS"`
and `complete_ready` is reachable only through `cmd_groundtruth`, so the old
"GroundTruth's step explicitly skipped" instruction was indeed unexecutable.

**Requirement 7 â€” wrappers and agent files.** Both new commands have
`.claude/commands/` wrappers, and the record-gate wrapper carries the same
notes-to-a-temp-file security note the other verdict wrappers use rather than
interpolating free text into a shell command. Dev Team 1, Dev Team 2 and
Master Controller are all updated, and the split is right: Dev Team runs the
lifecycle-mutating commands, Master Controller writes the requirement into the
sprint file and does not run them, matching CLAUDE.md's command-ownership
rule. QA1, Pipeman and GroundTruth gain no step and are correctly unchanged.

**Requirement 8 â€” no product code.** `git diff --name-only` over `app/`,
`lib/`, `components/`, `data/` is empty.

**Requirement 9 â€” no closed sprint's state touched.** Confirmed above: none of
the ten real state files carries `human_gates`.

===================================================================
THE REQUIRED FIX
===================================================================

**A gate PASS never goes stale, and four places say it does.** This is a
documentation defect in requirement 1's own deliverable, not a code defect â€”
which is why it is a CONDITIONAL and not a FAIL.

Reproduced in the sandbox, end to end:

  1. declare gate3 at `dev_build`
  2. record gate3 PASS ("AT pass on early build") â€” still at `dev_build`
  3. commit a substantial further change
  4. qa1 PASS -> dev-done -> ship -> groundtruth PASS -> complete_ready
  5. `complete` succeeds:
     "Sprint 3 closed. Confirmed: QA1 audit, GroundTruth live test, user
      authorization, Gate 3 (human AT pass, e.g. NVDA)."

The gate result carries no commit and no hash â€” the stored shape is
`{declared, result, rounds}` and nothing more â€” and no code path invalidates
it when the code changes. So a human accessibility pass run against one build
closes a sprint that shipped a different one, and the close line reports the
gate as confirmed.

Meanwhile the mechanism describes itself as enforcing the opposite. "A fresh
PASS on record" appears four times in `sprint_lifecycle.py` (module docstring,
`cmd_declare_gate`'s output, `cmd_record_gate`'s output, and `cmd_complete`'s
own refusal message) and in all three updated agent files, including the
instruction Dev Team acts on: *"Once QA1's audit and GroundTruth's live test
have both passed and every declared human gate has a fresh PASS on record,
tell the user the sprint is ready."* Nothing computes freshness. An agent
reading that sentence will believe the script checked something it did not.

I am not asking for the mechanism. Binding a gate result to a commit is a real
design decision with the same subtleties `qa1_audited_tree_hash` had to solve
â€” content rather than SHA, so a squash or a docs-only commit doesn't
spuriously invalidate a genuine pass â€” and inventing it inside this audit
would be exactly the in-flight substitution this project keeps refusing. It is
a new requirement, not a correction.

What requirement 1 does already demand is the record: *"Where a question is
answered 'no change needed', the reasoning is recorded the same way."* The
design records precisely this kind of reasoning for the two fields Q3
deliberately leaves alone. It records nothing about gate-result freshness, and
the surrounding language asserts a guarantee that does not exist.

FIX, and it is small:
  (a) State the limitation in the Q4 design: a recorded gate PASS is not bound
      to a commit, so it is the recorder's responsibility to run the gate
      against the code that will actually ship. Say why that is acceptable for
      now, the same way Q3 says why `last_shipped_commit` is left alone.
  (b) Stop the four "fresh PASS" sites and the agent-file instructions
      implying enforcement. "A PASS on record" is accurate; "a fresh PASS on
      record" is a claim about a check that isn't there. The Dev Team agent
      files are where this matters most â€” that is the sentence an agent acts
      on.

Why I am holding a verdict over wording: Sprint 10 turned on a single false
Dev Notes sentence, and I held a CONDITIONAL there for the same reason â€”
requirement 4 had made that analysis an audited deliverable, and a wrong
record is worse than no record because future work checks against it.
Requirement 1 makes this design an audited deliverable in exactly the same
way, and CLAUDE.md's own line applies: a standard that is actively wrong
produces confident incorrect predictions. This one would produce them in the
agents that run the lifecycle.

===================================================================
FOR MASTER CONTROLLER, NOT BLOCKING
===================================================================

Whether to bind a human-gate result to a commit is worth a decision rather
than a default. The case for it is this project's own history: Sprint 8 took
five rounds of ARIA changes *after* its human gate was added, and Sprint 9's
gate 3 found a real defect at the very end. Code changing after a human pass
is the norm here, not an edge case, and the QA1 tree-hash exists because this
project already learned that a stale PASS is dangerous. The case against is
that the design's minimalism is deliberate and well-argued, and a second hash
mechanism has its own failure modes. Either answer is defensible; drifting
into one is not. If the answer is "not worth it," that is exactly the shape of
answer requirement 1 asks to be recorded.

===================================================================
OBSERVATIONS â€” NO ACTION
===================================================================

- `smoke_test.sh` hardcodes `python3` and `/tmp`, and on this machine neither
  works: `python3` resolves to the Microsoft Store stub (`Python was not
  found`), and native Windows Python resolves `/tmp/x` to `C:\tmp\x` while
  Git Bash's `/tmp` is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp`. Both are **pre-existing** â€” I
  ran the pre-Sprint-12 suite as a control and it fails identically at the
  same line â€” and Dev Notes discloses both honestly rather than claiming a
  clean local run. The new tests follow the file's existing `/tmp` convention
  rather than introducing a new one, which is the right call for consistency.
  I got the suite passing with a `python3 -> python` shim on PATH and a
  temporary `C:\tmp` junction, both created and removed inside this audit;
  nothing on the machine or in the repo was left changed. Worth someone's
  time eventually so the suite is runnable here without undocumented local
  setup, but not this sprint's job and not a blocker.
- `cmd_dev_done`'s refusal after a reopen reads "Current phase: dev_build,
  QA1 result: PASS," which is momentarily confusing since the stated QA1
  result is a PASS. It is correct â€” the phase check is what blocks â€” and Q3
  argues deliberately for keeping `qa1_audit_result`. Pre-existing message
  text, not worth changing on its own.
- `override --gate gate3/gate4` has no phase guard, so a gate could be
  undeclared on an already-complete sprint. The realistic case is caught by
  the not-declared check, the action is human-confirmed and permanently
  logged, and the gate's recorded result survives it, so nothing can be made
  to look like a pass that wasn't. Noting it as considered, not as a defect.

===================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
===================================================================

Record the limitation and fix the four "fresh PASS" sites plus the agent-file
sentences, and this is a PASS. No code change, no test change, nothing to
rebuild â€” and I will re-run the suite and the sandbox scenarios on the
re-audit rather than carrying this round's results forward.

Then: gate 2 for this sprint is the non-regression plus scope-violation trap
the sprint file already scopes, and the trap is currently satisfiable â€”
`app/`, `lib/`, `components/` and `data/` are untouched, so GroundTruth should
find nothing user-visible to fail on. No gate 3 and no gate 4 apply, and this
sprint should declare neither, which is itself the first live test of Q2's
"declares no human gate" state.

This is good work. The design is argued rather than asserted, the rejected
alternatives are recorded with reasons, the implementation matches the design
everywhere I probed it, the new tests assert against state files rather than
success messages, the sandbox discipline that once destroyed a real project's
history twice is intact, and backward compatibility was verified against the
actual eleven state files instead of being assumed. The gap I am holding on is
one this sprint got close enough to see and did not quite name.
